title: light passed hand to hand
hookLine: fire that couldn't burn a blade of grass, and why Hindus offer a flame back to God

cards: Evening at a temple, or a living room when the lamp comes out. A small flame sits on a metal plate, and someone moves it in slow circles before the shrine. A bell rings.
People sing. Then the plate is carried around the room, and one by one, people pass their hands over the flame and bring their palms to their eyes and forehead. Why offer fire to God at all?
An old story has an answer.

teach.b: Arti: the waving of a lamp, the offering of light. The best-known song begins om jai jagadish hare: victory to you, lord of the world. Now the story, from one of the oldest Hindu texts.
The gods once won a great victory and grew proud: we did this. Then a strange being appeared before them, and nobody knew who it was. They sent Agni, the god of fire.
I can burn anything on earth, he boasted.

teach.h: FIRE COULDN'T BURN ONE BLADE OF GRASS
teach.b: The being set down a single blade of grass. Burn this. Agni rushed at it with everything he had, and couldn't burn it.
The god of the wind went next: I can blow away anything. He couldn't move the grass. Then Indra, king of the gods, came near, and the being vanished.
In its place stood a shining goddess, Uma, who told him: that was Brahman. The victory was Brahman's all along. Fire burns because of Brahman, not on its own.
Another old line says it: everything shines after that one shining, even this little fire. Many teachers read arti this way: a small flame is light offered back to where light comes from.

teach.h: THE SAME FIRE TOUCHES EVERY FACE
teach.b: Then it leaves the shrine and goes to the people, and each person draws its warmth to their eyes: the same fire for every face. Often prasad follows: food offered to God, handed back as a blessing.
Whatever shines in you, a gift, a good day, a win, the old answer is the same. It's borrowed light. Offer it back, then share it.

how: Arti is performed in temples and homes, often in the morning and evening: a lamp is waved before the image of God while a bell rings and a song is sung, and then the flame is brought to each person, who passes their hands over it and touches their eyes and forehead.

s: it happens in temples, at riverbanks and in living rooms, wherever the lamp comes out.
an old Hindu text says everything shines after that one shining
even the sun, moon and stars, it says, and this little fire.
the flame stays at the shrine
it's carried to the people, and each person draws its warmth toward their face.

games.q: in the reading this lesson gives, why is a small flame circled before the image of God?
o: to light up the shrine so people can see it.
to offer light back to where light comes from.
to keep the room warm during the song.
games.why: everything shines after that one shining, even this little fire. the flame goes back to its source, then comes out to every face.

practice: Three breaths with the bell. If there's a candle or a lamp near you, look at it; any light in the room will do. Cup your hands toward it, as if gathering warmth, and bring them to your eyes and forehead.
Then bring one person to mind and turn your cupped hands toward them, as if passing the plate.

wordCard.voice: Arti. The offering of light, and then the light shared with everyone. Fifth word.

orig.note: Hindi, from Sanskrit: the waving of a lamp before God, the offering of light.

carryVoice: Your line: light passed hand to hand. Next time the plate comes around, you'll know what you're doing. Day five.
